Please process the following webpage content and user goal to extract relevant information:

## **Webpage Content** 
Title: Magnetoreception

URL Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception

Published Time: 2005-02-14T22:57:36Z

Markdown Content:
"Magnetoception" redirects here. For the Joshua Abrams album, see [Magnetoception (album)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoception_(album) "Magnetoception (album)").

[![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Erithacus_rubecula_-RHS_Garden_Harlow_Carr-8c.jpg/500px-Erithacus_rubecula_-RHS_Garden_Harlow_Carr-8c.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Erithacus_rubecula_-RHS_Garden_Harlow_Carr-8c.jpg)

Experiments on [European robins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_robin "European robin"), which are [migratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_migration "Bird migration"), suggest their magnetic sense makes use of the quantum [radical pair mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_pair_mechanism "Radical pair mechanism"). 

**Magnetoreception** is a [sense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sense "Sense") which allows an [organism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organism "Organism") to detect the [Earth's magnetic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_magnetic_field "Earth's magnetic field").  Animals with this sense include some [arthropods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthropod "Arthropod"), [molluscs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollusc "Mollusc"), and [vertebrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebrate "Vertebrate") (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals).  The sense is mainly used for orientation and [navigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_navigation "Animal navigation"), but it may help some animals to form regional maps. Experiments on [migratory birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_migration "Bird migration") provide evidence that they make use of a [cryptochrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptochrome "Cryptochrome") protein in the eye, relying on the quantum [radical pair mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_pair_mechanism "Radical pair mechanism") to perceive magnetic fields. This effect is extremely sensitive to weak magnetic fields, and readily disturbed by radio-frequency interference, unlike a conventional iron compass. Some [bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteria "Bacteria") orient passively using [magnetite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetite "Magnetite") crystals; the mechanism has not been reliably detected in [eukaryotes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eukaryote "Eukaryote").

[Cartilaginous fish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartilaginous_fish "Cartilaginous fish") including [sharks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shark "Shark") and [stingrays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stingray "Stingray") can detect small variations in electric potential with their [electroreceptive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electroreception "Electroreception") organs, the [ampullae of Lorenzini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ampullae_of_Lorenzini "Ampullae of Lorenzini"). These appear to be able to detect magnetic fields by [induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_induction "Electromagnetic induction"). There is some evidence that these fish use magnetic fields in navigation.

Biologists have long wondered whether [migrating animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_migration "Animal migration") such as [birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_migration "Bird migration") and [sea turtles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_turtle_migration "Sea turtle migration") have an inbuilt magnetic compass, enabling them to [navigate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_navigation "Animal navigation") using the [Earth's magnetic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_magnetic_field "Earth's magnetic field"). Until late in the 20th century, evidence for this was essentially only [behavioural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethology "Ethology"): many experiments demonstrated that animals could indeed derive information from the magnetic field around them, but gave no indication of the mechanism. In 1972, Roswitha and Wolfgang Wiltschko showed that migratory birds responded to the direction and [inclination (dip)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_dip "Magnetic dip") of the magnetic field. In 1977, M. M. Walker and colleagues identified iron-based ([magnetite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetite "Magnetite")) magnetoreceptors in the snouts of [rainbow trout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_trout "Rainbow trout"). In 2003, G. Fleissner and colleagues claimed to have found iron-based receptors in the upper beaks of [homing pigeons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homing_pigeons "Homing pigeons"), but subsequent studies employing high resolution electron microscopy revealed that the cells identified are in fact macrophages.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Treiber2012-1) Research took a different direction in 2000, when Thorsten Ritz and colleagues suggested that a [photoreceptor protein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photoreceptor_protein "Photoreceptor protein") in the eye, [cryptochrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptochrome "Cryptochrome"), was a magnetoreceptor, working at a molecular scale by [quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement "Quantum entanglement").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Winklhofer_2010-2)

## Proposed mechanisms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Proposed mechanisms")]

### Passive iron-based alignment in bacteria

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Passive iron-based alignment in bacteria")]

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Magnetite_magnetosomes_in_Gammaproteobacteria.png/500px-Magnetite_magnetosomes_in_Gammaproteobacteria.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Magnetite_magnetosomes_in_Gammaproteobacteria.png)

[Magnetite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetite "Magnetite") magnetosomes in [Gammaproteobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gammaproteobacteria "Gammaproteobacteria") strain SS-5. (A) Chain of highly elongated magnetosomes. (B) Part of a chain. (C) The magnetosome in the lower right in (B), viewed along the ![Image 3: {\displaystyle \scriptstyle [1{\overline {1}}0]}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f99ce4c507bedc2d8c9e600715fe15e2d2666907) direction, with its [Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform "Fourier transform") in the lower right.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-3)

[Magnetotactic bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetotactic_bacteria "Magnetotactic bacteria") of multiple taxa contain sufficient magnetic material in the form of [magnetosomes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetosome "Magnetosome"), nanometer-sized particles of [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron")-containing [magnetite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetite "Magnetite"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-4) that the Earth's magnetic field passively aligns them, just as it does with a compass needle. The bacteria are thus not actually sensing the magnetic field.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-6)

A possible but unexplored mechanism of magnetoreception in animals is through [endosymbiosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endosymbiosis "Endosymbiosis") with magnetotactic bacteria, whose DNA is widespread in animals. This would involve having these bacteria living inside an animal, and their magnetic alignment being used as part of a magnetoreceptive system.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-7)

While numerous studies have claimed to identify magnetite-based magneotoreceptors in vertebrates such as birds,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Fleissner2003-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Falkenberg2010-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Hore_2016-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Solov'yov_Greiner_2007-11) none have been independently replicated; most have been shown to be iron-rich [macrophages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macrophage "Macrophage")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Treiber2012-1) or environmental contaminants.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-12)

In animals, the mechanism for magnetoreception is still under investigation. Three main hypotheses are currently being discussed: one proposing a quantum compass based on a [radical pair mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_pair_mechanism "Radical pair mechanism"),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-13) one postulating a iron-based magnetic compass with [magnetite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetite "Magnetite") particles,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Wiltschkojcp-14) and a third that relies on electromagnetic induction.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-15)

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Quantum_Magnetoreception_in_Birds.svg/960px-Quantum_Magnetoreception_in_Birds.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Quantum_Magnetoreception_in_Birds.svg)

The [radical pair mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_pair_mechanism "Radical pair mechanism") has been proposed for quantum magnetoreception in birds. It takes place in [cryptochrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptochrome "Cryptochrome") molecules in cells in the birds' [retinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retina "Retina").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)

According to the first model, magnetoreception is possible via the [radical pair mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_pair_mechanism "Radical pair mechanism"),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Hore_2016-10) which is well-established in [spin chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_chemistry "Spin chemistry"). The mechanism requires two molecules, each with unpaired electrons, at a suitable distance from each other. When these can exist in states either with their [spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_(physics) "Spin (physics)") axes in the same direction, or in opposite directions, the molecules oscillate rapidly between the two states. That oscillation is extremely sensitive to magnetic fields.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Rodgers_2009-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Steiner_Ulrich_1989-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Woodward_2002-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Rodgers_Hore_2009-20) Because the Earth's magnetic field is extremely weak, at 0.5 [gauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_(unit) "Gauss (unit)"), the radical pair mechanism is currently the only credible way that the Earth's magnetic field could cause chemical changes (as opposed to the mechanical forces which would be detected via magnetic crystals acting like a compass needle).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Rodgers_Hore_2009-20)

In 1978, Schulten and colleagues proposed that this was the mechanism of magnetoreception.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-21) In 2000, scientists proposed that [cryptochrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptochrome "Cryptochrome") – a [flavoprotein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flavoprotein "Flavoprotein") in the [rod cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_cell "Rod cell") in the eyes of birds – was the "magnetic molecule" behind this effect.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-22) It is the only protein known to form photoinduced radical-pairs in animals.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Hore_2016-10) The function of cryptochrome varies by species, but its mechanism is always the same: exposure to blue light excites an electron in a [chromophore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromophore "Chromophore"), which causes the formation of a radical-pair whose electrons are [quantum entangled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement "Quantum entanglement"), enabling the precision needed for magnetoreception.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Wiltschko_Ahmad_Nie%C3%9Fner_Gehring_2016-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-24)

Many lines of evidence point to cryptochrome and radical pairs as the mechanism of magnetoreception in birds:[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)

*   Despite 20 years of searching, no biomolecule other than cryptochrome has been identified capable of supporting radical pairs.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)
*   In cryptochrome, a yellow molecule [flavin adenine dinucleotide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flavin_adenine_dinucleotide "Flavin adenine dinucleotide") (FAD) can absorb a photon of blue light, putting the cryptochrome into an activated state: an electron is transferred from a tryptophan amino acid to the FAD molecule, forming a radical pair.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)
*   Of the six types of cryptochrome in birds, cryptochrome-4a (Cry4a) binds FAD much more tightly than the rest.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)
*   Cry4a levels in [migratory birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migratory_birds "Migratory birds"), which rely on navigation for their survival, are highest during the spring and autumn migration periods, when navigation is most critical.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)
*   The Cry4a protein from the [European robin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_robin "European robin"), a migratory bird, is much more sensitive to magnetic fields than similar but not identical Cry4a from pigeons and chickens, which are non-migratory.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)

These findings together suggest that the Cry4a of migratory birds has been [selected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_selection "Natural selection") for its magnetic sensitivity.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)

Behavioral experiments on migratory birds support this theory. Caged migratory birds such as robins display migratory restlessness, known by [ethologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethologist "Ethologist") as _[Zugunruhe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zugunruhe "Zugunruhe")_, in spring and autumn: they often orient themselves in the direction in which they would migrate. In 2004, Thorsten Ritz showed that a weak radio-frequency electromagnetic field, chosen to be at the same frequency as the singlet-triplet oscillation of cryptochrome radical pairs, effectively interfered with the birds' orientation. The field would not have interfered with an iron-based compass. Further, birds are unable to detect a 180 degree reversal of the magnetic field, something they would straightforwardly detect with an iron-based compass.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Effect_of_RF_interference_on_Magnetoreception_in_Birds.svg/960px-Effect_of_RF_interference_on_Magnetoreception_in_Birds.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Effect_of_RF_interference_on_Magnetoreception_in_Birds.svg)

Very weak [radio-frequency interference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_interference "Electromagnetic interference") prevents [migratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_migration "Bird migration") robins from orienting correctly to the [Earth's magnetic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_magnetic_field "Earth's magnetic field"). Since this would not interfere with an iron compass, the experiments imply that the birds use a radical-pair mechanism.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)

From 2007 onwards, Henrik Mouritsen attempted to replicate this experiment. Instead, he found that robins were unable to orient themselves in the wooden huts he used. Suspecting extremely weak radio-frequency interference from other electrical equipment on the campus, he tried shielding the huts with aluminium sheeting, which blocks electrical noise but not magnetic fields. When he earthed the sheeting, the robins oriented correctly; when the earthing was removed, the robins oriented at random. Finally, when the robins were tested in a hut far from electrical equipment, the birds oriented correctly. These effects imply a radical-pair compass, not an iron one.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)

In 2016, Wiltschko and colleagues showed that European robins were unaffected by [local anaesthesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_anesthesia "Local anesthesia") of the upper beak, showing that in these test conditions orientation was not from iron-based receptors in the beak. In their view, cryptochrome and its radical pairs provide the only model that can explain the avian magnetic compass.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Wiltschko_Ahmad_Nie%C3%9Fner_Gehring_2016-23) A scheme with three radicals rather than two has been proposed as more resistant to spin relaxation and explaining the observed behaviour better.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Kattnig_2017-25)

#### Electromagnetic induction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Electromagnetic induction")]

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Yellow_Stingray%2C_Belize%2C_2007-09.jpg/330px-Yellow_Stingray%2C_Belize%2C_2007-09.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yellow_Stingray,_Belize,_2007-09.jpg)

The [yellow stingray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_stingray "Yellow stingray") is able to sense the intensity and [inclination angle of a magnetic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_dip "Magnetic dip").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Newton_Gill_Kajiura_2020-26)

Another possible mechanism of magnetoreception in animals is electromagnetic induction in [cartilaginous fish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartilaginous_fish "Cartilaginous fish"), namely [sharks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shark "Shark"), [stingrays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stingray "Stingray"), and [chimaeras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimaera "Chimaera"). These fish have [electroreceptive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electroreception "Electroreception") organs, the [ampullae of Lorenzini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ampullae_of_Lorenzini "Ampullae of Lorenzini"), which can detect small variations in [electric potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_potential "Electric potential"). The organs are mucus-filled and consist of canals that connect pores in the skin of the mouth and nose to small sacs within the animal's flesh. They are used to sense the weak electric fields of prey and predators. These organs have been predicted to sense magnetic fields, by means of [Faraday's law of induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faraday's_law_of_induction "Faraday's law of induction"): as a conductor moves through a magnetic field an electric potential is generated. In this case the conductor is the animal moving through a magnetic field, and the potential induced (_V_ ind) depends on the time (t)-varying rate of magnetic flux (Φ) through the conductor according to ![Image 7: {\displaystyle V_{ind}=-{\frac {d\Phi }{dt}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/44c2f057ca79c6dc644bcaa129ade62cc1ffee90)

The ampullae of Lorenzini detect very small fluctuations in the potential difference between the pore and the base of the electroreceptor sac. An increase in potential results in a decrease in the rate of nerve activity. This is analogous to the behavior of a current-carrying conductor.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Anderson_Clegg_V%C3%A9ras_Holland_2017-29)[Sandbar sharks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandbar_shark "Sandbar shark"), _Carcharinus plumbeus_, have been shown to be able to detect magnetic fields; the experiments provided non-definitive evidence that the animals had a magnetoreceptor, rather than relying on induction and electroreceptors.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Anderson_Clegg_V%C3%A9ras_Holland_2017-29) Electromagnetic induction has not been studied in non-aquatic animals.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Rodgers_Hore_2009-20)

The [yellow stingray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_stingray "Yellow stingray"), _Urobatis jamaicensis_, is able to distinguish between the intensity and inclination angle of a magnetic field in the laboratory. This suggests that cartilaginous fishes may use the Earth's magnetic field for navigation.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Newton_Gill_Kajiura_2020-26)

## Unanswered questions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Unanswered questions")]

It remains likely that two or more complementary mechanisms play a role in magnetic field detection in animals. Of course, this potential dual mechanism theory raises the questions of to what degree each method is responsible for the stimulus, and how they produce a signal in response to the weak magnetic field of the Earth.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Rodgers_Hore_2009-20)

In addition, it is possible that magnetic senses may be different for different species. Some species may only be able to detect north and south, while others may only be able to differentiate between the equator and the poles. Although the ability to sense direction is important in migratory navigation, many animals have the ability to sense small fluctuations in earth's magnetic field to map their position to within a few kilometers.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Rodgers_Hore_2009-20)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-30)

Magnetoreception is widely distributed taxonomically. It is present in many of the animals so far investigated. These include [arthropods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthropod "Arthropod"), [molluscs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollusc "Mollusc"), and among [vertebrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebrate "Vertebrate") in fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Its status in other groups remains unknown.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Wiltschko-31)

The ability to detect and respond to magnetic fields may exist in plants, possibly as in animals mediated by cryptochrome. Experiments by different scientists have identified multiple effects, including changes to growth rate, seed [germination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germination "Germination"), [mitochondrial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitochondrion "Mitochondrion") structure, and responses to gravity ([geotropism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geotropism "Geotropism")). The results have sometimes been controversial, and no mechanism has been definitely identified. The ability may be widely distributed, but its taxonomic range in plants is unknown.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Maffei_2014-32)

The giant sea slug _[Tochuina gigantea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tochuina\_gigantea "Tochuina gigantea")_ (formerly _T. tetraquetra_), a [mollusc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollusc "Mollusc"), orients its body between north and east prior to a full moon.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Lohmann_Willows_1987-33) A 1991 experiment offered a right turn to geomagnetic south and a left turn to geomagnetic east (a [Y-shaped maze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y_maze "Y maze")). 80% of _Tochuina_ made a turn to magnetic east. When the field was reversed, the animals displayed no preference for either turn.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Wang_Cain_Lohmann_pp._1043%E2%80%931049-35)_Tochuina_'s nervous system is composed of individually identifiable [neurons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuron "Neuron"), four of which are stimulated by changes in the applied magnetic field, and two which are inhibited by such changes.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Wang_Cain_Lohmann_pp._1043%E2%80%931049-35) The tracks of the similar species _[Tritonia exsulans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tritonia\_exsulans "Tritonia exsulans")_ become more variable in direction when close to strong [rare-earth magnets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rare-earth_magnet "Rare-earth magnet") placed in their natural habitat, suggesting that the animal uses its magnetic sense continuously to help it travel in a straight line.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Wyeth_Holden_Jalala_Murray_2021-36)

The fruit fly _[Drosophila melanogaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drosophila\_melanogaster "Drosophila melanogaster")_ may be able to orient to magnetic fields. In one [choice test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preference_tests_(animals) "Preference tests (animals)"), flies were loaded into an apparatus with two arms that were surrounded by electric coils. Current was run through each of the coils, but only one was configured to produce a 5-Gauss magnetic field (about ten times stronger than the Earth's magnetic field) at a time. The flies were trained to associate the magnetic field with a sucrose reward. Flies with an altered cryptochrome, such as with an antisense mutation, were not sensitive to magnetic fields.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Gegear2008-37)

Magnetoreception has been studied in detail in insects including [honey bees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey_bee "Honey bee"), [ants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant "Ant") and [termites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Termite "Termite").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Pereira-Bomfim_2015-38) Ants and bees navigate using their magnetic sense both locally (near their nests) and when migrating.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Wajnberg_2010-39) In particular, the Brazilian stingless bee _[Schwarziana quadripunctata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarziana\_quadripunctata "Schwarziana quadripunctata")_ is able to detect magnetic fields using the thousands of hair-like [sensilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensillum "Sensillum") on its antennae.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Esquivel_2005-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Lucano_2005-41)

Studies of magnetoreception in [bony fish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bony_fish "Bony fish") have been conducted mainly with salmon. Both [sockeye salmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sockeye_salmon "Sockeye salmon") (_Oncorhynchus nerka_) and [Chinook salmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinook_salmon "Chinook salmon") (_Oncorhynchus tschawytscha_) have a compass sense. This was demonstrated in experiments in the 1980s by changing the axis of a magnetic field around a circular tank of young fish; they reoriented themselves in line with the field.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Quinn_1980-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Taylor_1986-43)

Some of the earliest studies of amphibian magnetoreception were conducted with [cave salamanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_salamander "Cave salamander") (_Eurycea lucifuga_). Researchers housed groups of cave salamanders in corridors aligned with either magnetic north–south, or magnetic east–west. In tests, the magnetic field was experimentally rotated by 90°, and salamanders were placed in cross-shaped structures (one corridor along the new north–south axis, one along the new east–west axis). The salamanders responded to the field's rotation.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-:Phillips_1977-44)

[Red-spotted newts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_newt "Eastern newt") (_Notophthalmus viridescens_) respond to drastic increases in water temperature by heading for land. The behaviour is disrupted if the magnetic field is experimentally altered, showing that the newts use the field for orientation.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Phillips_1986_newt-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Phillips_1986_salamander-46)

Both [European toads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_toad "Common toad") (_Bufo bufo_) and [natterjack toads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natterjack_toad "Natterjack toad") (_Epidalea calamita)_ toads rely on vision and olfaction when migrating to breeding sites, but magnetic fields may also play a role. When randomly displaced 150 metres (490 ft) from their breeding sites, these toads can navigate their way back,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-:12-47) but this ability can be disrupted by fitting them with small magnets.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-:6-48)

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Leatherback_Turtle_eggs_hatching_at_Eagle_Beach%2C_Aruba_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Leatherback_Turtle_eggs_hatching_at_Eagle_Beach%2C_Aruba_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leatherback_Turtle_eggs_hatching_at_Eagle_Beach,_Aruba_(cropped).jpg)

Magnetoreception plays a part in guiding [loggerhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggerhead_sea_turtle "Loggerhead sea turtle") hatchlings to the sea.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Lohmann_et_al_2022-49)

The majority of study on magnetoreception in reptiles involves turtles. Early support for magnetoreception in turtles was provided in a 1991 study on hatchling [loggerhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggerhead_sea_turtle "Loggerhead sea turtle") turtles which demonstrated that loggerheads can use the magnetic field as a compass to determine direction.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Lohmann_1991-50) Subsequent studies have demonstrated that loggerhead and green turtles can also use the magnetic field of the earth as a map, because different parameters of the Earth's magnetic field vary with geographic location. The map in sea turtles was the first ever described though similar abilities have now been reported in lobsters, fish, and birds.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Lohmann_et_al_2022-49) Magnetoreception by land turtles was shown in a 2010 experiment on _Terrapene carolina_, a [box turtle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_turtle "Box turtle"). After teaching a group of these box turtles to swim to either the east or west end of an experimental tank, a strong magnet disrupted the learned routes.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Mathis_Moore_2010-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Stehli_1996-52)

Orientation toward the sea, as seen in turtle hatchlings, may rely partly on magnetoreception. In [loggerhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggerhead_sea_turtle "Loggerhead sea turtle") and [leatherback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leatherback_sea_turtle "Leatherback sea turtle") turtles, breeding takes place on beaches, and, after hatching, offspring crawl rapidly to the sea. Although differences in light density seem to drive this behaviour, magnetic alignment appears to play a part. For instance, the natural directional preferences held by these hatchlings (which lead them from beaches to the sea) reverse upon experimental inversion of the magnetic poles.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Merrill_Salmon_2010-53)

[Homing pigeons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homing_pigeon "Homing pigeon") use magnetic fields as part of their complex [navigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_navigation "Animal navigation") system.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-54)[William Keeton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Tinsley_Keeton "William Tinsley Keeton") showed that time-shifted homing pigeons (acclimatised in the laboratory to a different time-zone) are unable to orient themselves correctly on a clear, sunny day; this is attributed to time-shifted pigeons being unable to compensate accurately for the movement of the sun during the day. Conversely, time-shifted pigeons released on overcast days navigate correctly, suggesting that pigeons can use magnetic fields to orient themselves; this ability can be disrupted with magnets attached to the birds' backs.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Gould,_J._L._1984-56) Pigeons can detect magnetic anomalies as weak as 1.86 [gauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_(unit) "Gauss (unit)").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-ReferenceA-57)

For a long time the [trigeminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigeminal_nerve "Trigeminal nerve") system was the suggested location for a magnetite-based magnetoreceptor in the pigeon. This was based on two findings: First, magnetite-containing cells were reported in specific locations in the upper beak.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Fleissner2003-8) However, the cells proved to be immune system [macrophages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macrophage "Macrophage"), not [neurons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuron "Neuron") able to detect magnetic fields.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Treiber2012-1)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Engels_20180124-58) Second, pigeon magnetic field detection is impaired by sectioning the trigeminal nerve and by application of [lidocaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lidocaine "Lidocaine"), an anaesthetic, to the olfactory mucosa.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-59) However, lidocaine treatment might lead to unspecific effects and not represent a direct interference with potential magnetoreceptors.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Engels_20180124-58) As a result, an involvement of the trigeminal system is still debated. In the search for magnetite receptors, a large iron-containing organelle (the [cuticulosome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuticulosome "Cuticulosome")) of unknown function was found in the inner ear of pigeons.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-61)

Areas of the pigeon brain found in a 2011 study to respond with increased activity to magnetic fields are the posterior [vestibular nuclei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestibular_nuclei "Vestibular nuclei"), [dorsal thalamus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorsal_thalamus "Dorsal thalamus"), [hippocampus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippocampus "Hippocampus"), and [visual hyperpallium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avian_pallium "Avian pallium"). The vestibular nuclei receive information from the inner ear including the [semicircular canals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semicircular_canals "Semicircular canals"). This suggests that bird sense magnetism in the inner ear.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-62) A 2025 study in _[Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science\_(journal) "Science (journal)")_ presents two lines of evidence that pigeons sense magnetic fields in their inner ears. Firstly, brain mapping found populations of neurons whose activity is triggered by magnetic fields. Neuron activity was measured using a genetic marker. Brain activity of pigeons exposed to a rotating magnetic field was found in the part of the brain linked to the semicircular canals, and other regions that collate sensory information. Secondly, RNA sequencing in single inner ear cells of the semicircular canals found "the molecular machinery necessary for the detection of magnetic stimuli by [electromagnetic induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_induction "Electromagnetic induction")."[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Nordmann_2025-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Castelvecchi_2025-64)

[Chickens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickens "Chickens") have iron mineral deposits in the sensory [dendrites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dendrites "Dendrites") in the upper beak and are capable of magnetoreception.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Falkenberg2010-9)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Wiltschko_et_al.,_2007-65) Beak trimming causes loss of the magnetic sense.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Freire_et_al.,_2011-66)

Superparamagnetic macrophages are present in the liver of pigeons. After macrophage depletion, pigeons flying under overcast conditions lacked their usual orientation capabilities. The superparamagnetic macrophages appear to be required for sensing magnetic direction.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-67)

Some mammals are capable of magnetoreception. When [woodmice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_mouse "Wood mouse") are removed from their home area and deprived of visual and olfactory cues, they orient towards their homes until an inverted magnetic field is applied to their cage.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-68) When the same mice are allowed access to visual cues, they are able to orient themselves towards home despite the presence of inverted magnetic fields. This indicates that woodmice use magnetic fields to orient themselves when no other cues are available. The magnetic sense of woodmice is likely based on a radical-pair mechanism.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-69)

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Graumull_IMG_4039.jpg/250px-Graumull_IMG_4039.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Graumull_IMG_4039.jpg)

The [Zambian mole-rat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambian_mole-rat "Zambian mole-rat") is one of several mammals that use magnetic fields, in their case for nest orientation.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Nemec_2001-70)

The [Zambian mole-rat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambian_mole-rat "Zambian mole-rat"), a subterranean mammal, uses magnetic fields to aid in nest orientation.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Marhold_Wiltschko_Burda-71) In contrast to woodmice, Zambian mole-rats do not rely on radical-pair based magnetoreception, perhaps due to their subterranean lifestyle. Experimental exposure to magnetic fields leads to an increase in neural activity within the [superior colliculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superior_colliculus "Superior colliculus"), as measured by immediate [gene expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_expression "Gene expression"). The activity level of neurons within two levels of the superior colliculus, the outer sublayer of the intermediate gray layer and the deep gray layer, were elevated in a non-specific manner when exposed to various magnetic fields. However, within the inner sublayer of the intermediate gray layer (InGi) there were two or three clusters of cells that respond in a more specific manner. The more time the mole rats were exposed to a magnetic field, the greater the immediate early gene expression within the InGi.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Nemec_2001-70)

Magnetic fields appear to play a role in [bat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bat "Bat") orientation. They use [echolocation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_echolocation "Animal echolocation") to orient themselves over short distances, typically ranging from a few centimetres up to 50 metres.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-72) When non-migratory big brown bats (_[Eptesicus fuscus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eptesicus\_fuscus "Eptesicus fuscus")_) are taken from their home roosts and exposed to magnetic fields rotated 90 degrees from magnetic north, they become disoriented; it is unclear whether they use the magnetic sense as a map, a compass, or a compass calibrator.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-73) Another bat species, the greater mouse-eared bat (_[Myotis myotis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myotis\_myotis "Myotis myotis")_), appears to use the Earth's magnetic field in its home range as a compass, but needs to calibrate this at sunset or dusk.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Holland_Borissov_Siemers_2010-74) In migratory soprano pipistrelles (_[Pipistrellus pygmaeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soprano\_pipistrelle "Soprano pipistrelle")_), experiments using mirrors and [Helmholtz coils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmholtz_coil "Helmholtz coil") show that they calibrate the magnetic field using the position of the solar disk at sunset.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-76)

[Red foxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_fox "Red fox") (_Vulpes vulpes_) may be influenced by the Earth's magnetic field when [predating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predation "Predation") small rodents like mice and voles. They attack these prey using a specific high-jump, preferring a north-eastern compass direction. Successful attacks are tightly clustered to the north.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-77)

There is not yet a consensus on whether humans can sense magnetic fields, but some evidence suggests it.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Wang_Hilburn_Wu_2019-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Chae_Human_magnetic_sense-79) The [ethmoid bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethmoid_bone "Ethmoid bone") in the nose contains magnetic materials.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Carrubba_Frilot-80)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Chae_Human_magnetic_sense-79) Magnetosensitive cryptochrome 2 (cry2) is present in the human retina.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Foley_2011-81) Human alpha [brain waves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain_wave "Brain wave") are affected by magnetic fields, but it is not known whether behaviour is affected.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Wang_Hilburn_Wu_2019-78)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception#cite_note-Foley_2011-81)

  "evidence": "Magnetoreception is a sense which allows an organism to detect the Earth's magnetic field. Animals with this sense include some arthropods, molluscs, and vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals). The sense is mainly used for orientation and navigation, but it may help some animals to form regional maps.

Experiments on migratory birds provide evidence that they make use of a cryptochrome protein in the eye, relying on the quantum radical pair mechanism to perceive magnetic fields. This effect is extremely sensitive to weak magnetic fields, and readily disturbed by radio-frequency interference, unlike a conventional iron compass.

Biologists have long wondered whether migrating animals such as birds and sea turtles have an inbuilt magnetic compass, enabling them to navigate using the Earth's magnetic field. Until late in the 20th century, evidence for this was essentially only behavioural: many experiments demonstrated that animals could indeed derive information from the magnetic field around them, but gave no indication of the mechanism.

In animals, the mechanism for magnetoreception is still under investigation. Three main hypotheses are currently being discussed: one proposing a quantum compass based on a radical pair mechanism, one postulating a iron-based magnetic compass with magnetite particles, and a third that relies on electromagnetic induction.

The radical pair mechanism has been proposed for quantum magnetoreception in birds. It takes place in cryptochrome molecules in cells in the birds' retinas.

Many lines of evidence point to cryptochrome and radical pairs as the mechanism of magnetoreception in birds:
*   Despite 20 years of searching, no biomolecule other than cryptochrome has been identified capable of supporting radical pairs.
*   In cryptochrome, a yellow molecule flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) can absorb a photon of blue light, putting the cryptochrome into an activated state: an electron is transferred from a tryptophan amino acid to the FAD molecule, forming a radical pair.
*   Of the six types of cryptochrome in birds, cryptochrome-4a (Cry4a) binds FAD much more tightly than the rest.
*   Cry4a levels in migratory birds, which rely on navigation for their survival, are highest during the spring and autumn migration periods, when navigation is most critical.
*   The Cry4a protein from the European robin, a migratory bird, is much more sensitive to magnetic fields than similar but not identical Cry4a from pigeons and chickens, which are non-migratory.

These findings together suggest that the Cry4a of migratory birds has been selected for its magnetic sensitivity.

Behavioral experiments on migratory birds support this theory. Caged migratory birds such as robins display migratory restlessness, known by ethologists as Zugunruhe, in spring and autumn: they often orient themselves in the direction in which they would migrate. In 2004, Thorsten Ritz showed that a weak radio-frequency electromagnetic field, chosen to be at the same frequency as the singlet-triplet oscillation of cryptochrome radical pairs, effectively interfered with the birds' orientation. The field would not have interfered with an iron-based compass. Further, birds are unable to detect a 180 degree reversal of the magnetic field, something they would straightforwardly detect with an iron-based compass.

Very weak radio-frequency interference prevents migratory robins from orienting correctly to the Earth's magnetic field. Since this would not interfere with an iron compass, the experiments imply that the birds use a radical-pair mechanism.

From 2007 onwards, Henrik Mouritsen attempted to replicate this experiment. Instead, he found that robins were unable to orient themselves in the wooden huts he used. Suspecting extremely weak radio-frequency interference from other electrical equipment on the campus, he tried shielding the huts with aluminium sheeting, which blocks electrical noise but not magnetic fields. When he earthed the sheeting, the robins oriented correctly; when the earthing was removed, the robins oriented at random. Finally, when the robins were tested in a hut far from electrical equipment, the birds oriented correctly. These effects imply a radical-pair compass, not an iron one.

In 2016, Wiltschko and colleagues showed that European robins were unaffected by local anaesthesia of the upper beak, showing that in these test conditions orientation was not from iron-based receptors in the beak. In their view, cryptochrome and its radical pairs provide the only model that can explain the avian magnetic compass.

In 1972, Roswitha and Wolfgang Wiltschko showed that migratory birds responded to the direction and inclination (dip) of the magnetic field.

While numerous studies have claimed to identify magnetite-based magneotoreceptors in vertebrates such as birds, none have been independently replicated; most have been shown to be iron-rich macrophages or environmental contaminants.

Homing pigeons use magnetic fields as part of their complex navigation system. William Keeton showed that time-shifted homing pigeons (acclimatised in the laboratory to a different time-zone) are unable to orient themselves correctly on a clear, sunny day; this is attributed to time-shifted pigeons being unable to compensate accurately for the movement of the sun during the day. Conversely, time-shifted pigeons released on overcast days navigate correctly, suggesting that pigeons can use magnetic fields to orient themselves; this ability can be disrupted with magnets attached to the birds' backs. Pigeons can detect magnetic anomalies as weak as 1.86 gauss.

Areas of the pigeon brain found in a 2011 study to respond with increased activity to magnetic fields are the posterior vestibular nuclei, dorsal thalamus, hippocampus, and visual hyperpallium. The vestibular nuclei receive information from the inner ear including the semicircular canals. This suggests that bird sense magnetism in the inner ear. A 2025 study in Science presents two lines of evidence that pigeons sense magnetic fields in their inner ears. Firstly, brain mapping found populations of neurons whose activity is triggered by magnetic fields. Neuron activity was measured using a genetic marker. Brain activity of pigeons exposed to a rotating magnetic field was found in the part of the brain linked to the semicircular canals, and other regions that collate sensory information. Secondly, RNA sequencing in single inner ear cells of the semicircular canals found 'the molecular machinery necessary for the detection of magnetic stimuli by electromagnetic induction.'

Magnetoreception is widely distributed taxonomically. It is present in many of the animals so far investigated. These include arthropods, molluscs, and among vertebrates in fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals.",

Behavioral experiments, including observations of migratory restlessness (Zugunruhe), support this mechanism. The page also discusses an alternative iron-based magnetite compass, but notes that many claims for such receptors have not been replicated. ## **Webpage Content** 
Title: The Magnetic Compass of Birds: The Role of Cryptochrome

URL Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2021.667000/full

Published Time: 2021-05-19

Markdown Content:
## Abstract

The geomagnetic field provides directional information for birds. The avian magnetic compass is an inclination compass that uses not the polarity of the magnetic field but the axial course of the field lines and their inclination in space. It works in a flexible functional window, and it requires short-wavelength light. These characteristics result from the underlying sensory mechanism based on radical pair processes in the eyes, with cryptochrome suggested as the receptor molecule. The chromophore of cryptochrome, flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), undergoes a photocycle, where radical pairs are formed during photo-reduction as well as during re-oxidation; behavioral data indicate that the latter is crucial for detecting magnetic directions. Five types of cryptochromes are found in the retina of birds: cryptochrome 1a (Cry1a), cryptochrome 1b, cryptochrome 2, cryptochrome 4a, and cryptochrome 4b. Because of its location in the outer segments of the ultraviolet cones with their clear oil droplets, Cry1a appears to be the most likely receptor molecule for magnetic compass information.

## The Geomagnetic Field

The geomagnetic field surrounding the Earth is generated mainly by the Earth itself. Its two poles lie close to the rotational (geographic) poles but are not identical with them. The magnetic field lines emerge from the pole in the South (which is a physical North pole), where they go straight upward, then run around the Earth and reenter its surface at the pole in the North. Near the geographic equator, they form the “magnetic equator,” being horizontal, parallel to the Earth’s surface. The angle between the field lines and the horizontal, called “inclination,” or “dip,” is defined as positive when it is downward as in the northern hemisphere and negative when it is upward; it is 0° at the magnetic equator and -90°, respectively, +90°, at the poles. Magnetic intensity (field strength) is low compared to technically applied fields; it is largest at the magnetic poles, where it is about 60 μT (microTesla) and decreases toward the magnetic equator, with a local low of 23 μT at the South American east coast. At Frankfurt am Main, Germany (50°N, 9°E), for example, the inclination today is about 67° and the total intensity about 47 μT (for more information, see ; ).

We humans need instruments like a technical compass for indicating directions and a magnetometer for measuring intensity. Many animals from a wide variety of groups, however, are directly sensitive to the geomagnetic field and can use its information for navigation. Birds are by far the best-studied group, and the respective findings indicate that they have two sensors for different qualities of the geomagnetic field: one based on chemical processes to obtain directional information from the course of the field lines to use as a compass and another one based on magnetite (a special form of Fe 3 O 4) to measure magnetic intensity as a component of the navigational mechanisms indicating the location (for an overview, see, e.g., ). Here, we will focus on the avian magnetic compass, its functional properties and what is presently known about the detection of magnetic directional information and the putative role of the cryptochrome.

## The Avian Magnetic Compass

The ability of birds to use compass information from the magnetic field was first described in the 1960s in migratory birds. During the migratory seasons in autumn and in spring, these birds have a strong urge to move into their innate migratory direction. They show this directional preference also in suitable test cages, and when the North direction of the magnetic field around the cage is shifted by a coil system, the bird changes its heading accordingly, maintaining the same magnetic bearing. This was first demonstrated in European Robins, _Erithacus rubecula_ (Turdidae), a small songbird (), but has meanwhile been shown in more than 20 other bird species from various avian lineages that are not closely related (for a list, see ). Among them are also a number of non-migrants, like, e.g., Homing Pigeons, _Columba livia domestica_, where it was demonstrated in homing experiments (; ) and by conditioning (). It was also demonstrated by directional training in Domestic Chickens, _Gallus gallus domesticus_ (Phasanidae; ), and Zebra Finches, _Taeniopygia guttata_, (Estrildidae; ; ). Using the geomagnetic field as a compass thus seems to be a general feature of birds that employ this compass for orientation within their home range as well as during migration (for review, see, e.g., , ).

The functional mode of the avian magnetic compass was also analyzed in behavioral experiments with migrating birds by exposing the test birds to different magnetic conditions and observing their responses. Three characteristics became evident:

*   **(1)**
The magnetic compass of birds does not sense the polarity of the magnetic field but the axial course of the field lines. It is a so-called _inclination compass_ that decides between the directions of this axis by the inclination of the field lines. For birds, the magnetic compass does not indicate magnetic North and South, as our technical compass does, but instead “poleward,” the direction where the field lines are tilted downward and “equatorward,” where they are pointing upward (). This type of magnetic compass was found in all bird species tested for it (see ).

*   **(2)**
The avian magnetic compass works only in a functional window around the local geomagnetic intensity, with fields more than about 20 to 25% weaker and stronger than the local field leading to disorientation. In particular, the disorientation in stronger fields was unexpected and seems unusual for stimuli. However, the functional window is not fixed but rather proved to be flexible: after staying in a field with higher or lower intensity, birds were able to orient at the respective intensity. European Robins caught and kept at 47 μT could adjust to fields as low as 4 μT and as high as 150 μT without losing their ability to oriented in the local field of 47 μT. (; ) Yet they could not orient in an intermediate field that they had not experienced before – it appears that staying in a field outside the original functional window creates a new functional window at the respective intensity (; ; ). A similar response to magnetic intensity was found in Domestic Chickens ().

*   **(3)**
The magnetic compass of birds is light-dependent (). It works in bright sunshine under the full spectrum light (see, e.g., ), but further studies showed that light from the short-wavelength end of the spectrum is required and that the light intensities necessary are very low. Birds were oriented under narrow-band light with a peak wavelength of 373 nm ultraviolet (UV), 424 nm blue, 501 nm turquoise, and 565 nm green light; under 568 nm and 585 nm yellow light and 617 nm, 635 nm, and 645 nm red light they were disoriented (; , ; ; ; ). These studies were done under rather low intensities (8 × 10 16 quanta s–1 m–2, see, e.g., ).

## The “Radical Pair” Model

These characteristics of the avian magnetic compass imply an unusual sensory mechanism, and they caused to propose the “Radical Pair”-model based on spin-chemical processes in photo-pigments that interact with the geomagnetic field. Absorption of photons leads to the formation of radical pairs, which can occur in two states, namely _singlet_ with antiparallel spin and _triplet_ with parallel spin, with the ratio singlet/triplet depending on the directional relation of the radical pair to the ambient magnetic field. Since the singlet and triplet products are different, this ratio could indicate magnetic directions. proposed the eyes as a site of magnetoreception because light is available and because of their round shape, the receptor cells are arranged in all spatial directions. This would result in a specific activation pattern across the retina that is centrally symmetric to the direction of the magnetic vector and thus can indicate the axis of the field lines. As photo-pigment mediating magnetic directions, cryptochrome was suggested because it is the only photo-pigment known in animals that forms radical pairs.

This model can explain the specific characteristics of the avian magnetic compass: Since the relationship of the radical pair to the field lines and thus the singlet/triplet ratio ignores the polarity of the field, the consequence is an inclination compass as found in birds. The fact that the activation pattern would change with intensity explains the flexible functional window; birds experiencing a sudden intensity change are faced with a novel activation pattern. This may at first be confusing; however, because the pattern retains its central symmetry to the magnetic vector, birds can eventually learn to interpret it. The dependency of magnetic compass orientation on short-wavelength light is largely in agreement with the absorbance spectrum of cryptochrome (see, e.g., ), which was found in the avian eyes (, ).

Experimental evidence meanwhile supports the Radical Pair-Model. In an electro-retinographic study, differences in responses to varying magnetic directions were recorded in the retina under blue, but not under red light (). Radio-frequency fields in the MHz (MegaHertz)-range are a diagnostic test for the involvement of radical pair processes (see, e.g., ; ); such radio-frequency fields indeed cause disorientation in birds ([Figure 1](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2021.667000/full#F1); e.g., , ; ; ; ). In a recent study, oscillating magnetic fields were applied directly to the eyes by a small battery-operated coil placed on the head of the bird; here, the birds remained oriented (). However, it is not clear whether their orientation was still based on their inclination compass or whether it involved a so-called “fixed direction response,” as they are frequently observed in situations where the normal inclination compass is disrupted (see for details and discussion).

## Cryptochrome Forming Radical Pairs

Cryptochromes are proteins with flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) as the chromophore (see, e.g., ; ). FAD undergoes a redox cycle that is best studied in plants; the oxidized form, FADox, is the dark resting form. Photon absorption of wavelengths from UV to about 500 nm blue photo-reduces FADox to the semiquinone FADH∙, forming a first radical pair with a tryptophan radical (Trp∙). FADH∙ can be re-oxidized independently of light, or, in a next step, it can be further photo reduced by light of wavelength from UV to green to FADH-, the fully reduced form. FADH- is then re-oxidized independently of light to FADox. During this step, a second radical pair is formed ([Figure 2](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2021.667000/full#F2)), possibly with O 2∙ (see, e.g., ; ), but the true partner of FADH∙ and details of this process are still under debate (see, e.g., ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ).

FIGURE 2

In view of this, the question arises which of the radical pairs would mediate the direction of the magnetic field. In plants, when cryptochromes are indicating the presence and amount of light for controlling biological processes like, e.g., hypocotyl growth or flowering, the radical pair formed during photo-reduction, FADH∙/Trp∙ is considered to be the crucial one. Green light, which reduces the amount of FADH∙ by further photo-reducing FADH∙ to the fully reduced state FADH-, was found to act antagonistically to blue light _in vitro_ as well as in living plants (e.g., ; ). However, in the case of the avian magnetoreception, the situation is different. Many birds—European Robins, Australian Silvereyes, _Zosterops l. lateralis_, Garden Warblers, _Sylvia borin_, and Zebra Finches—are oriented under narrow-band lights with peak wavelengths at blue as well as green light (, ; ; ). Since green light cannot photo-reduce FADox, this speaks against the involvement of the radical pair formed during photo-reduction being the one mediating magnetoreception but points to the other radical pair (see [Figure 2](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2021.667000/full#F2)).

Further behavioral experiments, however, showed that the orientation under green light is a transient phenomenon—it was possible only for less than 1 h. After this time, the birds were disoriented, whereas they continued to be oriented under the blue and turquoise light, that is, under wavelengths that can be absorbed by oxidized flavin. Also, orientation under green light was possible only when the birds had been before under “white” light, which included wavelengths that could photo-reduce oxidized cryptochrome—after staying in total darkness for 1 h, the birds were disoriented under green light, but they showed oriented headings under blue and turquoise light where the entire FAD-cycle can run (). This suggests that avian orientation under green light is possible only as long as there is a certain supply of FADH∙ available for further photo-reduction to the fully reduced FADH- by green light and again implies that the radical pair formed during light-independent re-oxidation is the one that mediates magnetic directions in birds.

To test this hypothesis, birds were exposed to flickering light and a pulsed magnetic field in the following manner: With a frequency of 1 Hz, light was available for 300 ms with the magnetic field compensated; during the remaining time, there was total darkness, but, except for security intervals of 10 ms at the beginning and the end, the geomagnetic field was present. In this situation, the birds showed oriented behavior ([Figure 3](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2021.667000/full#F3); ). This clearly shows that the actual process of sensing magnetic directions can occur in darkness—it identifies the radical pair formed during re-oxidation as the crucial one for sensing directions. Light, however, is necessary for photo-reduction to provide the fully reduced form FADH- that is re-oxidized for the formation of this radical pair.

FIGURE 3

This is different from what is known about cryptochrome when it controls light-dependent processes in plants; here, the radical pair FADH∙/Trp∙ is important because FADH∙ is formed, which was found to be the crucial form to indicate light. In the case of avian magnetoreception, however, radical pairs are to indicate the direction of the (geo)magnetic field. This is a different task, and it seems conceivable that evolution developed a modified mechanism that is better suited for this function.

In the future, it may help our understanding of cryptochromes and their functions if more attention was given to the re-oxidation process. A recent study () suggests that magnetic effects in plants can also be mediated by processes during re-oxidation in the dark; yet here, not the direction, but the intensity of the magnetic field was effective.

## Cryptochromes in the Avian Eyes

In the eyes of birds, five types of cryptochromes – cryptochrome 1a (Cry1a), cryptochrome 1b (Cry1b), cryptochrome 2 (Cry2), Cryptochrome 4a (Cry4a), and Cryptochrome 4b (Cry4b) – have been found (see also ).

Cryptochrome 1 was first described in birds by based on mRNA expression in the photoreceptor layer and the ganglion cell layer of chickens (see also ; ). In Robins, identified two splice products of the _Cry1_ gene, Cry1a and Cry1b; they differ in their _C_-termini, which suggests different functions. In an immuno-histochemical study, located Cry1a in the outer segments of the ultraviolet/violet (UVS/VS, SW1) cones in the retinae of Chickens and European Robins where immuno-marking for electron microscopy shows it positioned along the disks, where also the UV-opsin is located ([Figure 4](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2021.667000/full#F4)). described Cry1a in the outer segments of the UV/V cones also in pigeons, Blackcaps, _Sylvia atricapilla_, and Zebra Finches, so Cry1a in these locations appears to be common in all birds. Cell fractionation revealed Cry1a in the membrane fraction, suggesting that Cry1a is anchored along membranes (). In birds, photoreceptor cells contain oil droplets that absorb different amounts of short wavelengths in order to shift the maximum absorbance of the color receptors further apart for better color vision. Only the UVS/VS cones have clear oil droplets that allow all wavelengths of light to pass (see ). This type of photoreceptor is present all across the retina, i.e., in different directional relationships to the magnetic vector; hence they can give rise to the activation pattern suggested by ).

In contrast to Cry1a, Cry1b was located by immuno-histochemistry in the cytosol of ganglion cells, displaced ganglion cells, and also in the inner segments of the photoreceptors, free as well as bound to membranes (; ; ). In night-migrating birds, its expression varies with the season; it was much stronger during the migratory season when the birds were active during the night (; ). It has been speculated that Cry1b possibly plays a role in magnetoreception (), but, because the use of a magnetic compass appears to be a general sensory ability of birds, also shared by non-migrants (see above), the seasonal changes suggest another role—one that possibly involves the shift from diurnal activity to nocturnal activity (_Zugunruhe_) by night migrants.

It was found in a number of organs, among them the pineal gland and, in the eyes, in the photoreceptors, and in ganglion cells. This cryptochrome includes a sequence that suggests a location in the cell nucleus (; ), indicating a possible role as clock protein (see, e.g., for discussion of this role of cryptochromes).

Cryptochrome 4 was described in the retina of chickens first by using mRNA-expression and immuno-histochemistry (see also ). could identify Cry4 in the outer segments of the longwave-sensitive (LWS) single cones and of the double cones of European Robins. Recently, an isoform of Cry4, Cry4b, was identified by analyzing the DNA sequence. This splice product appears to be widespread; by genomic BLAST database search, it was also indicated in more than 25 avian species of various orders (). Another study localized Cry4 also in the outer plexiform layer, where it seemed associated with the synapses between photoreceptors and horizontal cells ().

A possible role of Cry4 in magnetoreception has been frequently discussed (e.g., ; ; ). Especially its location within the double cones prompted speculations on such a role of Cry4 because of the possibility that the input of two adjacent receptors with the magneto-receptive molecules oriented in different directions could be compared; it was proposed that this might help to overcome problems with different light intensities and polarization (; ). However, the principal cone is associated with an oil droplet that acts as a cut-off filter absorbing short wavelengths () and thus most of the wavelengths required for cryptochrome photo-reduction. This, together with the gap junctions between the two cones, would interfere with a comparison, making such a role of Cry4 in the double cones rather unlikely. speculated about a possible role of Cry4 in the outer plexiform layer. The Cry4 in the LWS single cones seems even less suitable for magnetoreception because the red oil droplets in these cones transmit only long wavelengths that cannot photo-reduce cryptochrome. Moreover, a study by implies that Cry 4 requires a very long time for re-oxidation, which would not be favorable for receptive processes.

Altogether, if cryptochrome is indeed the receptor molecule in birds, the presently available evidence indicates Cry1a as the most likely receptor for sensing directions. The observation that its gene expression shows a diurnal rhythm () does not speak against such a role, because it only indicates a rhythmic production in the inner segment of the cones, but it does not say anything about its general availability in the sensory active outer segment and its use. It appears to be a parallel case to vision, where the production of the visual pigment opsin also shows a diurnal pattern (e.g., ; ), but animals can see the entire day.

## Outlook

More than 50 years after the discovery of the avian magnetic compass, we finally have a concrete idea about the primary mechanism leading to the detection of directions by the magnetic field in birds: a radical pair process, with cryptochrome playing a crucial role in this process. Yet there are still several conflicting findings that have to be resolved, and a number of open questions that have to be answered.

One of the most important questions concerns the mechanisms by which the information obtained by the radical pair is transformed into a biological signal. Cryptochrome is found in the outer segments of cones, i.e., in a cell type that is also important for color vision. Is the visual information from the opsin and information on magnetic directions from cryptochrome transmitted separately or together? One might expect the latter since the cone has only one known way of transmitting information. This would mean, however, the two types of information have somehow to be separated, either already in the eyes or later in higher centers in the brain. There are speculations about possibilities (see, e.g., ), but it will require many more considerations and experiments until we hopefully reach a complete understanding of how birds perceive the direction of the geomagnetic field.

  "evidence": "## Abstract

The geomagnetic field provides directional information for birds. The avian magnetic compass is an inclination compass that uses not the polarity of the magnetic field but the axial course of the field lines and their inclination in space. It works in a flexible functional window, and it requires short-wavelength light. These characteristics result from the underlying sensory mechanism based on radical pair processes in the eyes, with cryptochrome suggested as the receptor molecule. The chromophore of cryptochrome, flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), undergoes a photocycle, where radical pairs are formed during photo-reduction as well as during re-oxidation; behavioral data indicate that the latter is crucial for detecting magnetic directions. Five types of cryptochromes are found in the retina of birds: cryptochrome 1a (Cry1a), cryptochrome 1b, cryptochrome 2, cryptochrome 4a, and cryptochrome 4b. Because of its location in the outer segments of the ultraviolet cones with their clear oil droplets, Cry1a appears to be the most likely receptor molecule for magnetic compass information.

## The Geomagnetic Field

... Many animals from a wide variety of groups, however, are directly sensitive to the geomagnetic field and can use its information for navigation. Birds are by far the best-studied group, and the respective findings indicate that they have two sensors for different qualities of the geomagnetic field: one based on chemical processes to obtain directional information from the course of the field lines to use as a compass and another one based on magnetite (a special form of Fe 3 O 4) to measure magnetic intensity as a component of the navigational mechanisms indicating the location (for an overview, see, e.g., ). Here, we will focus on the avian magnetic compass, its functional properties and what is presently known about the detection of magnetic directional information and the putative role of the cryptochrome.

## The Avian Magnetic Compass

The ability of birds to use compass information from the magnetic field was first described in the 1960s in migratory birds. During the migratory seasons in autumn and in spring, these birds have a strong urge to move into their innate migratory direction. They show this directional preference also in suitable test cages, and when the North direction of the magnetic field around the cage is shifted by a coil system, the bird changes its heading accordingly, maintaining the same magnetic bearing. ...

Three characteristics became evident:
- (1) The magnetic compass of birds does not sense the polarity of the magnetic field but the axial course of the field lines. It is a so-called inclination compass...
- (2) The avian magnetic compass works only in a functional window around the local geomagnetic intensity... However, the functional window is not fixed but rather proved to be flexible: after staying in a field with higher or lower intensity, birds were able to orient at the respective intensity. ...
- (3) The magnetic compass of birds is light-dependent. It works in bright sunshine under the full spectrum light... Birds were oriented under narrow-band light with a peak wavelength of 373 nm ultraviolet (UV), 424 nm blue, 501 nm turquoise, and 565 nm green light; under 568 nm and 585 nm yellow light and 617 nm, 635 nm, and 645 nm red light they were disoriented.

## The “Radical Pair” Model

These characteristics of the avian magnetic compass imply an unusual sensory mechanism, and they caused to propose the “Radical Pair”-model based on spin-chemical processes in photo-pigments that interact with the geomagnetic field. ... This model can explain the specific characteristics of the avian magnetic compass: Since the relationship of the radical pair to the field lines and thus the singlet/triplet ratio ignores the polarity of the field, the consequence is an inclination compass as found in birds. The fact that the activation pattern would change with intensity explains the flexible functional window; birds experiencing a sudden intensity change are faced with a novel activation pattern. This may at first be confusing; however, because the pattern retains its central symmetry to the magnetic vector, birds can eventually learn to interpret it. ... Experimental evidence meanwhile supports the Radical Pair-Model. ... Radio-frequency fields in the MHz (MegaHertz)-range are a diagnostic test for the involvement of radical pair processes (see, e.g., ; ); such radio-frequency fields indeed cause disorientation in birds ...

## Cryptochrome Forming Radical Pairs

Cryptochromes are proteins with flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) as the chromophore ... In view of this, the question arises which of the radical pairs would mediate the direction of the magnetic field. ... behavioral experiments ... suggest that the radical pair formed during light-independent re-oxidation is the one that mediates magnetic directions in birds. ... This clearly shows that the actual process of sensing magnetic directions can occur in darkness—it identifies the radical pair formed during re-oxidation as the crucial one for sensing directions. Light, however, is necessary for photo-reduction to provide the fully reduced form FADH- that is re-oxidized for the formation of this radical pair.

## Cryptochromes in the Avian Eyes

In the eyes of birds, five types of cryptochromes ... have been found. ... Altogether, if cryptochrome is indeed the receptor molecule in birds, the presently available evidence indicates Cry1a as the most likely receptor for sensing directions. ...",
